matter_reference_date_basis: exam_session APRIL 2018 recorded in candidates/matters/M107.json; the instruments in the scenario were executed on 4th June 2001, so the law is taken as it stood at the April 2018 session unless a provision was changed after that date.
corpus_gaps: No statutory rule of construction of deeds is in the corpus. The competition between the recital, the operative clause and the schedule of Deed of Gift No. 409 is governed by Roman-Dutch common law and judicial authority (falsa demonstratio, the primacy of the operative clause, the resolution of a repugnancy between operative clause and schedule), none of which is statutory or present in the frozen corpus.
The maxim nemo dat quod non habet, on which Waruni's position against Asanka ultimately turns, is a common-law principle and is not enacted in any Act in the corpus.

The Pradeshiya Sabha Act, No. 15 of 1987 is not in the corpus, so the local-authority limb referred to in Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16)(a) cannot be read in full; only the Municipal Councils Ordinance and the Urban Councils Ordinance limbs are available.

The corpus text of Notaries Ordinance s.31 is a consolidation carrying amendments up to 2024 (Act No. 31 of 2022 and Act No. 6 of 2024). The corpus does not expose the wording of rule (16) as it stood in April 2018, so that rule is recorded here as supporting only and is marked not applicable to the matter date.

The corpus does not contain a form or schedule prescribing the layout of a land schedule, so the drafted schedule below is built from the particulars listed in section 13 rather than from a statutory precedent.

provisions.why_relevant: This is the provision the question names. It fixes the particulars any schedule to Deed No. 429 must carry: an accurate and clear description of the land, its boundaries, its extent, its situation with the district and the village/pattu/korale or other division, and, the land being at Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla, the name of the street.

Subsection (2) is therefore engaged and adds a requirement over and above subsection (1): the divided portion itself must be defined by its own particular boundaries and its own extent, not merely by reference to the parent Lot C.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: Waruni's title to Lot C4 depends first on how much of Lot C passed to Asanka under Deed of Gift No. 409, and only then on whether Nimal had anything left to give by Deed No. 429. The first step is a pure question of construction of a deed whose recital is narrow (the building 'Waters Edge' No. 400A and the land whereon it stands), whose operative clause is ambiguous (a lot bearing Assessment No. 400A situated in Lot C, referred to the schedule) and whose schedule describes the whole 32-perch Lot C containing two buildings. The rules that resolve such a repugnancy - the primacy of the operative clause, falsa demonstratio non nocet, and the use of the schedule to identify the corpus of the grant - are Roman-Dutch common law and judicial authority, not statute, and none of them is in the corpus. The second step, that a donor cannot give what he no longer owns, is the common-law maxim nemo dat quod non habet, also not enacted in the corpus. The statutes in the corpus contribute only at the margins: they confirm that both deeds are registrable instruments affecting land, and they show that the statutory priority rule cannot decide the contest because neither donee took on valuable consideration. A complete answer therefore cannot rest on statute alone.

legal_issues.issue: On the true construction of Deed of Gift No. 409, did Nimal gift to Asanka the entirety of Lot C (32 perches, with both buildings Nos. 400 and 400A), or only the building 'Waters Edge' No. 400A and the land on which it stands?
If Deed No. 409 exhausted Nimal's interest in Lot C, could Deed No. 429 of the same date pass any title in Lot C4 to Waruni, given that a donor cannot convey an interest he has already parted with?
Can the statutory registration priority in the Registration of Documents Ordinance decide the contest between Deed No. 409 and Deed No. 429, both being deeds of gift executed on 4th June 2001?
Does Waruni's claim, if it succeeds at all, extend to the buildings bearing Assessment Nos. 400 and 400A, or only to so much of them as stands within the 10 perches of Lot C4?

questions.hop_count_basis: No indispensable statutory provision is recorded, because the determinative steps (construction of Deed No. 409 and the nemo dat consequence) are non-statutory. The statutory contribution is a single hop: section 8(b) brings both deeds within the registration Chapter, and section 7(1) read with section 7(4) then shows that the Chapter cannot resolve the contest. Hop count is set to 0 to record that no statutory chain carries the answer.

enrichment.original_background:
By a Deed of Gift bearing No.409 dated 4th June 2001 attested by G.W. de Silva Notary Public Nimal the Donor gifted his son Asanka No. 400A, "Waters Edge" Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla a house and property. The relevant clauses in the Deed of Gift are as follows. Recital All that building called "Waters Edge" bearing Assessment No.400A together with the land whereon the said building is situated free of all encumbrances whatsoever. Operative Clause All that allotment of land with the building standing thereon bearing Assessment No.400A situated in the said lot marked "C" and which said Lot "C" is morefully described in the schedule hereto.. Schedule All that allotment of land marked Lot Cin Plan No.450B dated 18th May 2000 made by Anil Silva, Licensed Surveyor of the land called Dawatagahawatta with the building called "Waters Edge" bearing Assessment No.400A standing thereon situated in the said allotment of land which contains two buildings bearing Assessment Nos.400 and 400A in extent of 32 perches.

After dividing Lot 'C' by Survey Plan No.450 B dated 18th May 2000, by Deed bearing No. 429 dated 4th June 2001 Nimal sub divided Lot C and gifted to his daughter Waruni Lot 'C4' in extent of 10 perches. Asanka claims the entirety of Lot 'C' including the buildings bearing Assessment Nos.400A and 400.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Waruni holds good title to Lot C4, 10 perches in extent, as against Asanka, and whether any such title carries the buildings bearing Assessment Nos. 400 and 400A. This turns on how much of Lot C passed to Asanka under Deed of Gift No. 409 of 4th June 2001, and on whether Nimal retained anything capable of being gifted by Deed No. 429 of the same date.
gold_answer_draft.rule: So far as the statutes in the corpus go: both deeds of gift are instruments affecting land, because Registration of Documents Ordinance s.8(b) treats as affecting land every instrument which purports or operates to create, confer, declare, limit, assign or transfer any right, title or interest in or over land, and 'land' in s.3 of that Ordinance includes things attached to the earth, so the buildings on Lot C are part of the land described. The registration Chapter therefore applies to Deed No. 409 and Deed No. 429 alike, and 'duly registered' under s.14(2) means registered in the folio proper to the land affected. But the statutory priority rule in s.7(1) protects only a party claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration under a subsequent duly registered instrument, and s.7(4) states in terms that registration confers on an instrument no effect or validity which it would not otherwise have, apart from that priority. The rules that would actually decide the contest - how a narrow recital, an ambiguous operative clause and a wider schedule are reconciled in a deed, and the principle that a donor cannot pass an interest he has already divested - are not statutory and are not in this corpus, so no complete answer can be given from statute.
gold_answer_draft.application: Deed No. 409 gifted to Asanka property described inconsistently across its three clauses: the recital speaks only of the building 'Waters Edge' No. 400A and the land whereon it stands; the operative clause speaks of an allotment with the building No. 400A standing thereon situated in Lot C, and refers to the schedule; the schedule describes Lot C in Plan No. 450B, of 32 perches, containing two buildings Nos. 400 and 400A. Which of these controls is the whole contest, and it is a matter of the construction of the deed rather than of any section of any Act in this corpus. Waruni's Deed No. 429 bears the same date, 4th June 2001, and gifts Lot C4 of 10 perches out of the same Lot C. Because both instruments are gifts, neither donee claims on valuable consideration, so neither can take the benefit of s.7(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance against the other, whichever was registered first; and s.7(4) prevents Waruni from arguing that registration of Deed No. 429 itself perfected a title. The question whether Waruni's 10 perches carry the buildings Nos. 400 and 400A is also open on the record, because the material does not state where within Lot C those buildings stand relative to Lot C4, although s.3 of the Ordinance confirms that whatever building stands on the ground included in a lot forms part of the land described.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: No statute-only answer can be given. The statutes establish only that both deeds are registrable instruments affecting land and that the registration priority rule cannot decide between two gifts. Whether Waruni has good title to Lot C4 as against Asanka depends on the construction of Deed of Gift No. 409 and on the common-law rule that a donor cannot give what he no longer has, neither of which is available in this corpus. The question is reserved for authority beyond the frozen statutory corpus. Nothing here has been validated by a lawyer.

answer_claims.claim_text: Both Deed of Gift No. 409 and Deed of Gift No. 429 are instruments affecting land within the registration Chapter of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, because s.8(b) covers every instrument which purports or operates to create, confer, declare, limit, assign or transfer any right, title or interest in or over land.

'Land' for the purposes of the Registration of Documents Ordinance includes things attached to the earth, so the buildings bearing Assessment Nos. 400 and 400A form part of the land described in a deed that includes the ground on which they stand.

The priority given by s.7(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance to a subsequent duly registered instrument runs only in favour of a party claiming an adverse interest on valuable consideration.
Registration under the Ordinance cures no defect in an instrument and confers on it no effect or validity it would not otherwise have, apart from the priority given by s.7 itself.

Since Deed No. 409 to Asanka and Deed No. 429 to Waruni are both deeds of gift, neither donee claims on valuable consideration, so neither can take the benefit of the s.7(1) priority against the other whichever deed was registered first.
Waruni cannot argue that registration of Deed No. 429 by itself gave her a title that the deed would not otherwise have carried.

The decisive question, namely how much of Lot C passed under Deed No. 409 given the conflict between its narrow recital, its ambiguous operative clause and its wider schedule, cannot be answered from any provision in the frozen statutory corpus.

Whether Waruni has good title to Lot C4 as against Asanka, and whether that title extends to the buildings bearing Assessment Nos. 400 and 400A, cannot be resolved on statutory authority alone and is reserved.

questions.block_reason: The answer turns on the construction of Deed of Gift No. 409 (recital versus operative clause versus schedule) and on the common-law principle that a donor cannot convey what he has already parted with. Neither rule is statutory and neither is in the frozen corpus; the only statutory priority rule, Registration of Documents Ordinance s.7, does not apply because both competing instruments are gifts rather than dispositions for valuable consideration. Reserved for a source of non-statutory authority.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: The question is a drafting task whose content is set by the statute it names. Section 13 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance itself lists every particular a schedule must carry, subsection (2) supplies the extra requirement for a divided portion such as Lot C4, and subsection (5) supplies the sanction for omission. No judicial authority or common-law doctrine is needed to identify the required particulars or to lay them out. The contested question of how much of Lot C passed to Asanka does not have to be decided in order to draft a schedule to Deed No. 429 that complies with section 13.

By a Deed of Gift bearing No.409 dated 4th June 2001 attested by G.W. de Silva Notary Public Nimal the Donor gifted his son Asanka No. 400A, "Waters Edge" Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla a house and property. The relevant clauses in the Deed of Gift are as follows. Recital All that building called "Waters Edge" bearing Assessment No.400A together with the land whereon the said building is situated free of all encumbrances whatsoever. Operative Clause All that allotment of land with the building standing thereon bearing Assessment No.400A situated in the said lot marked "C" and which said Lot "C" is morefully described in the schedule hereto.. Schedule All that allotment of land marked Lot Cin Plan No.450B dated 18th May 2000 made by Anil Silva, Licensed Surveyor of the land called Dawatagahawatta with the building called "Waters Edge" bearing Assessment No.400A standing thereon situated in the said allotment of land which contains two buildings bearing Assessment Nos.400 and 400A in extent of 32 perches.

After dividing Lot 'C' by Survey Plan No.450 B dated 18th May 2000, by Deed bearing No. 429 dated 4th June 2001 Nimal sub divided Lot C and gifted to his daughter Waruni Lot 'C4' in extent of 10 perches. Asanka claims the entirety of Lot 'C' including the buildings bearing Assessment Nos.400A and 400.

gold_answer_draft.issue: What must the schedule to Deed of Gift No. 429 dated 4th June 2001, by which Nimal gifted Lot C4 of 10 perches to Waruni, contain in order to satisfy section 13 of the Registration of Documents Ordinance, and how should that schedule be drafted?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Registration of Documents Ordinance s.13(1) requires every instrument other than a will presented for registration to contain, embodied in it or in a schedule annexed to it, an accurate and clear description of the land affected, giving its boundaries, its extent, and its situation specifying the district and the village, pattu, korale or other division of the district, and, where the land is in a town, the name of the street. Section 13(2) adds that where the land is a divided portion of a land or allotment, that portion must be clearly and accurately defined by its own particular boundaries and extent. Section 13(3), which requires the fractional proportion and a description of the entire land, applies only to an undivided share and is not engaged. By s.3 of the same Ordinance 'land' includes things attached to the earth, so any building standing on the lot forms part of what is described. Section 13(5) requires the Registrar to refuse registration of an instrument that does not state these particulars, subject to the appeal in s.13(5A) and (5B), and s.13(7) requires a reference to the volume and folio of the earlier registered instrument relating to the same land to be written at the head of the deed. Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (16) imposes the same description duty on the attesting notary and in its present form calls in addition for the Divisional Secretary's Division, the local authority division and the Grama Niladhari Division.
gold_answer_draft.application:
Lot C4 is a divided portion of Lot C, cut out by the sub-division of Lot C on Plan No. 450B dated 18th May 2000 made by Anil Silva, Licensed Surveyor, so both s.13(1) and s.13(2) apply and the lot must be defined by its own four boundaries and its own extent of 10 perches, not merely by reference to the 32-perch parent lot. The land lies at Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla, so the street name must appear. A compliant schedule may be drafted as follows.

THE SCHEDULE ABOVE REFERRED TO

All that divided allotment of land marked Lot C4 depicted in Plan No. 450B dated 18th May 2000 made by Anil Silva, Licensed Surveyor, of the land called Dawatagahawatta, situated at Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla, in the Grama Niladhari Division of [.....], in the [.....] pattu / korale, within the Divisional Secretary's Division of [.....] and within the administrative limits of the [.....] local authority, in the District of [.....], [.....] Province; and which said Lot C4 is bounded on the North by [.....], on the East by [.....], on the South by [.....] and on the West by [.....], and containing in extent Ten Perches (0A. 0R. 10P.) according to the said Plan No. 450B, together with the buildings, trees, plantations and everything else standing thereon.

Registered in Volume [.....] Folio [.....] of the [.....] Land Registry.

The bracketed particulars are the ones the facts given do not supply: the four boundaries of Lot C4, the district and the administrative divisions, and the volume and folio of the earlier registered deed. They must be taken from Plan No. 450B and from the folio in which Lot C stands registered before the deed is engrossed; without them the description is not accurate and clear within s.13(1) and the divided portion is not defined by its particular boundaries within s.13(2). The facts also do not state whether either building, No. 400 or No. 400A, stands on the 10 perches of Lot C4; if one does, its assessment number must be recited in the schedule, because by s.3 the building is part of the land conveyed. Whether Nimal in fact retained Lot C4 to gift after Deed No. 409 is a separate question and does not affect the form of the schedule.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: The schedule set out above states the particulars required by s.13(1) and s.13(2) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance: the lot number and the plan with its date and surveyor, the name of the land, the situation with the street, the administrative divisions and the district, the four boundaries of the divided portion, its extent of 10 perches, and what stands on it. On those particulars being completed the Registrar has no ground to refuse registration under s.13(5), and the volume and folio reference required by s.13(7) must also be written at the head of Deed No. 429. This draft is unverified and awaits a lawyer's review.

answer_claims.claim_text: Every instrument other than a will presented for registration must contain, in the instrument or in a schedule annexed to it, an accurate and clear description of the land affected, its boundaries, its extent and its situation specifying the district and the village, pattu, korale or other division of the district, and where the land is in a town the name of the street.
Where the land is a divided portion of a land or allotment, that portion must be clearly and accurately defined by its own particular boundaries and extent.
The requirement to state a fractional proportion and to describe the entire land applies only where the subject of the instrument is an undivided share, and so does not apply to a defined lot.
'Land' under the Registration of Documents Ordinance includes things attached to the earth, so a building standing on the lot is part of what the schedule describes.
The Registrar must refuse to register an instrument that does not state the particulars required by section 13.
A reference to the volume and folio in which an earlier instrument relating to the same land is registered must be written at the head of the deed presented for registration.

The attesting notary is separately forbidden to attest a deed affecting land unless the deed or an annexed schedule carries an accurate and clear description showing boundaries, extent and situation with the administrative divisions, and unless a divided share is defined by its particular boundaries and extent.

Lot C4 is a divided portion of Lot C created on Plan No. 450B dated 18th May 2000 by Anil Silva, Licensed Surveyor, so the schedule to Deed No. 429 must define Lot C4 by its own four boundaries and its own extent of 10 perches rather than by reference to the 32-perch parent lot.
Because the land lies at Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla, the schedule must give the street name as well as the district and the division of the district in which the land is situated.

The four boundaries of Lot C4, the district and administrative divisions, and the volume and folio of the earlier registered deed are not supplied by the facts and must be taken from Plan No. 450B and the land registry folio before the deed is engrossed; the schedule is left with marked blanks for them.

If either building, Assessment No. 400 or No. 400A, stands within Lot C4, its assessment number must be recited in the schedule, since the building forms part of the land described; the facts do not state where the buildings stand relative to Lot C4.

A schedule to Deed No. 429 describing all that divided allotment of land marked Lot C4 in Plan No. 450B dated 18th May 2000 made by Anil Silva, Licensed Surveyor, of the land called Dawatagahawatta, situated at Akuregoda Road, Pelawatta, Battaramulla, within the stated division and district, bounded on the North, East, South and West as shown on that plan, containing in extent ten perches, together with the buildings and everything standing thereon, states the particulars required by section 13(1) and section 13(2).

Once those particulars are completed the Registrar has no ground under section 13(5) to refuse registration, and the volume and folio reference required by section 13(7) must in addition be written at the head of Deed No. 429.

questions.block_reason: The question is still answerable from statute alone, but the gold answer states the wrong version of the operative provision. Section 13(1) of the Registration of Documents Ordinance was repealed and substituted by the Registration of Documents (Amendment) Act, No. 48 of 2011, s.2, which was in force at the April 2018 reference date; the rule statement and claim CL-M107-Q04-001 recite the superseded 1927 list and omit the Divisional Secretary's Division, the local authority division, the Grama Niladari Division and, for land in a municipality, town or developed area, the number as well as the street name. The drafted schedule carries most of those particulars only because they were taken from the notarial rule rather than from section 13, and it carries no assessment number. The prose needs a lawyer to restate the rule on the 2011 text before this can be gold.
